title: Environmental uncertainty shapes human effort learning
experiments_summary: Thirty-five right-handed healthy participants (28 included after exclusions) performed a novel effort learning task using hand-held dynamometers. Participants squeezed dynamometers to reach a hidden effort target displayed as a thermometer, with no explicit information about the required force level. The task used a 2x2 within-subject design manipulating volatility (low: 3 mean-effort changes per block; high: 7 changes per block) and noise (low: uniform distribution ±0.05 MVC; high: ±0.1 MVC). Participants completed 8 blocks (4 conditions × 2 hands), each comprising 48 trials. Individual maximum voluntary contraction (MVC) was calibrated before the experiment. Three dependent measures were extracted from continuous force traces: (1) start reaction time (RT), defined as time from thermometer onset to squeeze onset, measured via derivative thresholding; (2) effort prior, defined as force level at the first plateau in the force ramp, identified via smoothed absolute derivative minima; and (3) adjustment RT, defined as time from effort prior to steady-state force, detected via a sliding-window summed-derivative approach. Statistical analyses included: linear regression models for start RT and adjustment RT with regressors encoding volatility, noise, previous effort, jump sign, and jump size, with group-level inference via one-sample t-tests on beta coefficients; repeated-measures ANOVAs on beta weights from prior regression models fit separately per condition using past three trials' effort as regressors; a model-agnostic reinforcement learning approach estimating learning rates via linear regression of prior updates on prediction errors, with a 2-way ANOVA comparing learning rates across conditions; and Pearson correlations between individual learning rate changes and adjustment RT changes across uncertainty conditions. Control analyses examined long-term fatigue effects on start RT via slope estimation across block pairs, the contribution of online sensorimotor feedback to prior estimation, and adjustment RT effects restricted to non-change trials and separated into early versus late trial phases within constant-effort segments.
